Microprocessor Study Guide · Chapter 05

Build complete 8086 assembly programs

Connect declarations, program layout and control flow with working DOS input/output: character echo, case conversion, line input, stack reversal and decimal length output.

Scope: session 5 (13/04) · original 8086 · DOS-compatible real mode · Intel/MASM syntax · emu8086.

Start readingTry the exercises

One offline HTML file with 12 original slide illustrations, five worked applications, COM/EXE Hello templates, revision exercises and two tools. Select a figure to enlarge it.

00 · Turn individual instructions into a complete program

A useful assembly program needs more than a correct ADD or MOV. It needs a layout that the loader understands, initialized segment registers, a defined input/output interface, and control flow that reaches the intended exit. This session builds those pieces and applies them to five small DOS programs.

Prerequisites: data transfer and stacks, flags and branches, and state-tracing revision. Code uses Intel/MASM-style syntax for the original 8086 in a DOS-compatible environment such as emu8086. These DOS services are operating-system interfaces, not features supplied by every machine that executes an INT instruction.

  • Declare values and arrays and predict their byte layout.
  • Explain COM/EXE startup, the PSP, DS initialization and termination.
  • Build selection, counted, while and repeat-until structures.
  • Read the register contract of a DOS service and preserve live values.
  • Read, echo, convert, reverse and measure an ASCII line safely.

01 · Carry forward the instruction rules that programs depend on

Keep instruction meaning, encoding, operand width and timing separate. They answer different questions about the same line of code.

Revision pointCorrect rule
8086 versus 8088Both execute 16-bit word operations. The 8088’s external data bus is 8 bits, so word transfers need more bus activity; its instruction queue is 4 bytes versus 6 on the 8086.
Conditional branchesOn the original 8086, direct Jcc destinations are short displacements within the current CS. This restriction must not be generalized to all later x86 forms.
Mnemonic aliasesSigned JGE=JNL and JG=JNLE. Unsigned JA=JNBE. Do not replace a signed condition with an unsigned one merely because the English descriptions sound similar.
NEG and parityNEG BX with BX=34AEh gives CB52h. CF=1, SF=1 and PF=0: PF counts only the low result byte 52h, which contains three ones.
Set a bitOR AX,8000h sets the MSB without changing the other bits. XOR would toggle it rather than guarantee it is set.
Stack orderingPUSH decrements SP by two before storing a word; POP reads the word before increasing SP by two.
INT / IRETA software INT saves FLAGS, CS and next IP; IRET restores IP, CS and FLAGS. Clearing IF does not suppress an explicit INT or NMI.

Encode a memory load from fields, not from a memorized byte string

For MOV CX,[BX+DI+32DEh], the register/memory MOV opcode is 100010dw, with d=1 and w=1 → 8Bh. The second byte is 10 001 001: disp16, register CX, and address BX+DI → 89h. The displacement is little-endian, so the complete bytes are 8B 89 DE 32. The instruction occupies four bytes; an otherwise similar disp8 form occupies three.

Clock counts depend on the exact instruction form

The classic 8086 register-to-register MOV BL,CL has a documented baseline of two clocks. At 5 MHz, two clocks correspond to 0.4 microseconds. A memory MOV, a different operand width in a DIV, a taken branch, bus wait states or instruction fetching can change the relevant timing. An emulator’s animation speed is not a measurement of original processor timing.

The lecture also revisits processor classification. Its course taxonomy groups graphics work with signal processing; that does not make GPU and DSP programming models interchangeable. Likewise, a reduced instruction set alone does not prove lower energy consumption for every workload.

02 · Read a source statement as name, operation, operands and comment

A typical line has optional naming and explanation around its operation. In Intel syntax, a two-operand instruction places the destination first.

again:  add ax, bx      ; accumulate the next term
        jnz again      ; branch using the ZF left by the previous operation
count   db 5           ; a byte variable, not an instruction label
LIMIT   equ 80         ; a symbolic constant

again: is a branch label. count names stored data and normally has no colon in this declaration. LIMIT names a value at assembly time. A bare name is not automatically an instruction or a call. Use short ASCII identifiers beginning with a letter or underscore, and avoid reserved register/instruction names. The slides use older identifier-length conventions; using at most 31 characters is a conservative choice for these examples.

Literal notation changes the value

Written valueMeaningDecimal value
10Decimal integer10
10hHexadecimal integer16
1010bBinary integer10
0ABhHex literal with a leading digit to distinguish it from an identifier171
'9'ASCII character code57 (39h)

Quoted strings preserve their characters and case. In MASM-style declarations, both single and double quotes can delimit character data; “single quotes for a character, double quotes for a string” is not a universal assembler rule. Comments begin with a semicolon outside a quoted string.

Lecture: 30:00–38:00 (approximate). See sources and corrections.

03 · Distinguish stored data from assembly-time definitions

DB, DW and DD define elements of 1, 2 and 4 bytes. EQU gives a symbol an assembly-time value. These statements are not CPU operations, but some of them still place bytes in the program image.

limit    equ 80
flag     db 4
saved    db ?
word1    dw 1234h
wide     dd 12345678h
message  db 'Hello',13,10,'$'
zeros    db 4 dup(0)
DeclarationStorage / initialized bytes
flag DB 4One byte: 04h.
saved DB ?One byte of storage with no value the program may rely on before writing it.
word1 DW 1234hTwo bytes in ascending addresses: 34h,12h.
wide DD 12345678hFour bytes: 78h,56h,34h,12h. An 8086 can process it as two words.
limit EQU 80No byte allocated merely for this constant.

Do not interpret a question mark as “the variable is zero”. Initialize a value before using it. Do not interpret “directive rather than instruction” as “produces no bytes”: initialized DB/DW/DD declarations emit data bytes that the CPU could accidentally decode as instructions if execution falls into them.

For a declared byte, use byte registers or BYTE PTR as required. For a declared word, use a matching word operation. A declaration records a size for the assembler; it does not add runtime type checks to the 8086.

Lecture: 37:00–41:00 (approximate). See sources and corrections.

04 · Flatten arrays and expand DUP before calculating addresses

Array elements occupy consecutive storage in declaration order. DW elements advance by two bytes, and DD elements by four; DB advances by one.

values db 4,5,6,7,8,9
zeros  db 100 dup(0)
work   db 100 dup(?)
mixed  db 4,3,2,2 dup(1,2 dup(5),6)
; mixed expands to: 4,3,2,1,5,5,6,1,5,5,6

Expand the innermost repetition first. Here 2 DUP(5) gives 5,5; the outer repetition copies the whole sequence 1,5,5,6 twice. Including the initial 4,3,2 gives 11 bytes. DUP is performed during assembly; it is not a loop executed by the CPU.

Choose dimensions explicitly for a matrix

A 2×3 byte matrix with rows (1,6,3) and (4,2,5) is stored as 1,6,3,4,2,5. For zero-based row r and column c, its element offset is base + r×3 + c. For a word matrix with the same dimensions, multiply the element index by two.

Request in that 2×3 matrixElement indexByte displacement / word displacement
Row 0, column 222 / 4
Row 1, column 033 / 6
Row 1, column 255 / 10

There is no automatic second dimension in a sequence of DB declarations. Keep the column count and element size consistent in the address calculation, and validate indices before accessing storage. The memory addresses printed in the slide are an illustration rather than a required load address.

Lecture: 40:00–49:00 (approximate). See sources and corrections.

05 · Choose a layout convention and reserve a deliberate stack

The classic memory models describe how code and data are organized and how near/far references are used. The directive does not itself allocate all the computer’s memory or make a large array safe to index across a segment boundary.

ModelCode organizationData organization
TinyOne combined segment for code, data and stackCommon starting point for a DOS COM image.
SmallOne code segmentNear data within a 64-KiB group.
MediumMultiple code segmentsNear data within a 64-KiB group.
CompactOne code segmentMultiple data segments with far references.
LargeMultiple code segmentsMultiple data segments.
HugeMultiple code/data segmentsConventions can support larger objects, with suitable pointer/index handling.

.STACK 100 requests 100 decimal bytes; .STACK 100h requests 256 bytes. The MASM .STACK directive with no size has a documented default of 1 KiB. Omitting the directive entirely is a different case and does not guarantee an equivalent usable stack.

Budget for all active pushes, nested near/far return addresses, saved registers and interrupt frames. Original 8086 PUSH takes a word register or memory word; do not use PUSH AL or assume a later immediate-PUSH instruction is available. An image that stores one character per pushed word spends two stack bytes per character.

Lecture: 50:00–57:00 (approximate). See sources and corrections.

06 · Establish the loading assumptions before accessing a variable

A program segment prefix (PSP) is a 256-byte DOS structure containing process information. It is not the same as the EXE file header on disk. COM and EXE loading use it differently.

QuestionConventional DOS COMDOS MZ EXE
Entry pointOffset 0100h in the PSP segment.CS:IP is established from the executable header.
Initial data segmentsDS/ES conventionally refer to the same PSP segment as CS.DS/ES initially refer to the PSP, not necessarily the program’s data.
StackShares the segment; initial SP depends on the allocated block and loader conventions.SS:SP comes from the executable header.
Common initializationORG 100h sets assembled offsets.MOV AX,@data; MOV DS,AX establishes data access. Initialize ES separately if needed.
DOS 2+ terminationINT 21h with AH=4Ch works.INT 21h with AH=4Ch works.

@data is an assembler/linker symbol for the data group’s segment value. It is not a general-purpose variable. A segment register cannot receive an immediate with an ordinary MOV, hence the temporary AX. LEA DX,message loads an offset; it does not initialize DS for you.

A complete EXE Hello template

.model small
.stack 100h
.data
message db 13,10,'Hello from 8086!',13,10,'$'
.code
main proc
    mov ax, @data
    mov ds, ax
    lea dx, message
    mov ah, 09h
    int 21h
    mov ax, 4C00h
    int 21h
main endp
end main

main PROC/main ENDP delimit a source procedure. END main marks the module end and entry symbol; it is not a runtime exit instruction. The real termination is the INT 21h call with AX=4C00h: AH selects exit and AL supplies return code 0.

The equivalent COM layout

org 100h
jmp start
message db 13,10,'Hello from 8086!',13,10,'$'
start:
    lea dx, message
    mov ah, 09h
    int 21h
    mov ax, 4C00h
    int 21h

ORG changes the assembly-time origin; it does not execute a jump, allocate a PSP or add 256 padding bytes to this flat image. The initial JMP skips stored message bytes so the CPU starts with real code. INT 20h appears in the source’s COM template, but it requires the proper PSP segment in CS; function 4Ch is a convenient termination method for both formats.

The traditional build path is source → assembler object → linker executable; a tiny-model toolchain can produce COM directly. emu8086 combines much of that workflow. Renaming an EXE to .COM does not convert its format.

Lecture: 57:00–78:00 (approximate). See sources and corrections.

07 · Build selection with a comparison, branches and a join point

A conditional branch consumes flags produced by a comparison or test. Choose signed branches for signed quantities and unsigned branches for byte codes or unsigned magnitudes.

If-then: form an absolute magnitude

mov bx, ax
cmp bx, 0
jge nonnegative
neg bx
nonnegative:
; BX is the unsigned magnitude of signed AX; AX is unchanged.

The minimum signed word, AX=8000h (−32768), produces BX=8000h and OF=1 from NEG. That bit pattern is a valid unsigned magnitude of 32768, but not a positive signed word. If the caller requires a signed positive result, handle this case or widen the representation.

cmp ax, bx         ; compare signed words
jl is_less
mov cx, 1          ; else: AX >= BX
jmp joined
is_less:
mov cx, 0          ; then: AX < BX
joined:

JMP is essential here: the else path must not fall through into the then assignment. Conversely, neither CMP nor JL overwrites AX/BX. If the operands represent unsigned values, replace JL with JB to ask the corresponding unsigned question.

Three-way selection

cmp ax, 0
jl negative
je zero
mov cx, 1          ; the remaining case is AX > 0
jmp selected
negative:
mov cx, -1
jmp selected
zero:
xor cx, cx
selected:

For this sign classification, the positive case includes AX=1. A condition written AX>1 would omit that input. Put a join after the alternatives and check that every valid input reaches exactly one result assignment.

Lecture: 78:00–89:00 (approximate). See sources and corrections.

08 · Decide whether the test belongs before or after the body

A counted loop uses a fixed number of iterations

mov cx, 80
jcxz finished
emit_dollar:
mov dl, '$'
mov ah, 02h
int 21h
loop emit_dollar
finished:

LOOP decrements CX and branches when it is nonzero without rewriting FLAGS. The JCXZ guard makes an initial zero count skip the body. Function 02h prints the dollar sign normally; it is function 09h that treats dollar as a terminator.

A while loop may perform zero iterations

xor ax, ax
xor bx, bx
check_again:
cmp ax, 10
je while_done
inc bx
add ax, 2
jmp check_again
while_done:
; AX=10, BX=5

Starting at zero and adding two reaches ten after five body executions. Starting at an odd value and repeatedly adding two can never reach this even target, even after 16-bit wraparound. Choose a condition that matches the intended range/termination argument.

A repeat-until loop performs the body at least once

read_again:
mov ah, 01h
int 21h
cmp al, 13         ; decimal 13 = 0Dh = carriage return
jne read_again

The first read happens before the comparison. Reload AH inside the loop to make the service choice explicit. This reads an ordinary byte at a time; it is not a complete line editor. For editable line input, use the buffered service in section 12.

Lecture: 89:00–99:00 (approximate). See sources and corrections.

09 · Treat INT 21h as a collection of separate interfaces

INT 21h transfers control to DOS. AH usually chooses the function; the remaining input and output registers depend on that function. A register used as an input is not automatically a promised output or preserved temporary.

AHPurposeRequired inputsResult / effect
01hRead a character with echoAH=01h.AL receives its byte code. Ordinary keyboard input is echoed. An extended-key prefix may require another read.
02hWrite one characterDL=character code.Writes the character to standard output; DL is an input.
09hWrite a terminated stringDS:DX points to bytes ending in 24h (dollar).Writes bytes before the first dollar; the terminator is not printed.
0AhRead an editable buffered lineDS:DX points to an initialized buffer header and sufficient storage.Writes a count, input bytes and final CR into that buffer.
4ChTerminate process (DOS 2+)AL=exit code.Returns to the parent process; it does not return to the next instruction.

DOS standard input/output can be redirected, so “keyboard” and “screen” describe the default interactive setting used here. These programs target ordinary ASCII console use; they are not Unicode text programs.

Newlines are two control bytes

CR is decimal 13=0Dh and returns to the start of the line. LF is decimal 10=0Ah and advances a line. Use DB 13,10,'$' for a DOS string containing CR/LF. 10h is decimal 16 and is not LF. Function 09h does not append a newline automatically.

Preserve a live value before calling another service

Do not assume AL still holds a character after function 09h merely because the manual lists no formal return value. Preserve it in your own storage, a suitable saved register, or a balanced stack slot. The lecture demonstrates this exact failure before fixing the echo example.

10 · Application 1: read a character and echo the saved value

The first program writes a prompt, reads one ordinary character, writes a second prompt, and outputs the saved character. The read already echoes the keystroke; the explicit output after the second prompt is a second display.

org 100h
jmp start
prompt db 'Type one character: $'
answer db 13,10,'You typed: $'
saved  db ?
start:
    lea dx, prompt
    mov ah, 09h
    int 21h
    mov ah, 01h
    int 21h
    mov [saved], al        ; save before another service call
    lea dx, answer
    mov ah, 09h
    int 21h
    mov dl, [saved]
    mov ah, 02h
    int 21h
    mov ax, 4C00h
    int 21h
StageValue to keepWhy
After AH=01hAL holds the input.It is the result of the input service.
Before AH=09h for the second messagesaved stores that byte.The following DOS call must not be trusted to preserve live AL.
Before AH=02hDL reloads saved.The output service takes the character in DL.

Try A, 4 and a space as independent runs. The visible result after “You typed:” must match the input. For a stack-based variant, PUSH AX immediately after reading and POP AX before copying AL into DL; make sure AH is then reloaded to select output. Do not POP directly over an unrelated return address.

Lecture: 122:00–138:00 (approximate). See sources and corrections.

11 · Application 2: validate the ASCII range before subtracting 20h

Lowercase ASCII a…z occupy 61h…7Ah, while A…Z occupy 41h…5Ah. Only within that letter range does subtracting 20h implement the requested conversion.

org 100h
jmp start
prompt db 'Type a lowercase ASCII letter: $'
answer db 13,10,'Uppercase: $'
saved  db ?
start:
    lea dx, prompt
    mov ah, 09h
    int 21h
read_letter:
    mov ah, 01h
    int 21h
    test al, al
    jnz check_letter
    mov ah, 01h           ; consume the second byte of an extended key
    int 21h
    jmp read_letter
check_letter:
    cmp al, 'a'
    jb read_letter
    cmp al, 'z'
    ja read_letter
    sub al, 20h
    mov [saved], al
    lea dx, answer
    mov ah, 09h
    int 21h
    mov dl, [saved]
    mov ah, 02h
    int 21h
    mov ax, 4C00h
    int 21h

JB and JA compare the input byte as an unsigned code. The two bounds are inclusive: a and z are both accepted. The input is saved after conversion and before the message call. Invalid bytes cause another read rather than an arbitrary subtraction from a digit or control code.

InputAction
a / zPrint A / Z.
0 / A / {Read again; these are outside lowercase a…z.
Extended-key prefix 00hConsume the following code and read again.
A byte at or above 80hReject it as outside the ASCII lowercase range.

The program is a byte-range exercise. It does not implement locale-sensitive case conversion, accented letters, Unicode case folding or a polished retry prompt. For already validated ASCII letters, clearing bit 5 also maps lowercase to uppercase; validation remains necessary before using that shortcut on arbitrary input.

Lecture: 138:00–150:00 (approximate). See sources and corrections.

12 · Buffered input starts with a two-byte header

Function 0Ah does not accept an arbitrary uninitialized character array. The pointer must identify a structure whose first byte tells DOS how much input storage is available.

line db 81,0,81 dup(?)
; byte 0: 81 = space for up to 80 user characters plus a final CR
; byte 1: returned count, initialized to zero before the first read
; byte 2 onward: characters followed by CR
lea dx, line
mov ah, 0Ah
int 21h
Offset from lineMeaning after typing ABC and EnterByte value
+0Capacity including the final CR81 decimal (51h)
+1Number of user characters, excluding CR3 (03h)
+2 / +3 / +4A / B / C41h / 42h / 43h
+5Terminating carriage return0Dh

That declaration reserves 83 bytes: two header bytes plus 81 input-area bytes. For N desired user characters, reserve N+3 bytes and set byte 0 to N+1. The one-byte capacity allows at most 254 user characters under this convention. DOS provides interactive editing; byte 1 reports the edited line’s length, not a count of every keypress.

Initializing every byte to dollar is not the buffer contract. In DB 200 DUP('$'), the first byte becomes 24h, meaning capacity 36 rather than 200. The second byte is also an unintended 24h. The example may appear to work for a short line, but correct code sets the two header bytes deliberately.

Input termination and output termination are different

0Ah stores CR; it does not append dollar. For a dollar-terminated echo, replace line+2+count with '$' and point AH=09h at line+2. This still truncates at any dollar already inside the user’s input. The complete echo program below instead outputs exactly the returned count with AH=02h.

Inspect a DOS line buffer

Enter printable ASCII only. The model represents an edited line; it does not simulate keystrokes, Ctrl-C or redirection. Oversized input is rejected here rather than modeling DOS’s beep/ignore behavior.

For AB$ with capacity 8: header bytes 09h,03h; text 41h,42h,24h; final CR 0Dh. A counted echo prints AB$, while a dollar-terminated echo stops after AB.

Lecture: 150:00–163:00 (approximate). See sources and corrections.

13 · Application 3: echo exactly the returned line length

This version uses DOS line editing and a bounded input area. The output loop uses the returned count, so a dollar inside the input remains a normal character.

org 100h
jmp start
prompt db 'Type a line (up to 80 characters): $'
answer db 13,10,'You typed: $'
line   db 81,0,81 dup(0)
start:
    lea dx, prompt
    mov ah, 09h
    int 21h
    lea dx, line
    mov ah, 0Ah
    int 21h
    lea dx, answer
    mov ah, 09h
    int 21h
    xor cx, cx
    mov cl, [line+1]
    jcxz finish
    lea si, line+2
emit:
    mov dl, [si]
    mov ah, 02h
    int 21h
    inc si
    loop emit
finish:
    mov ax, 4C00h
    int 21h

Zero CX before loading CL: the count is a byte, but LOOP tests the whole CX. The JCXZ guard handles an empty line without entering a body that would underflow the count. SI addresses the first user character at line+2; the two header bytes are never printed.

Test an empty line, Hello, AB$CD and a full 80-character line. Neither the final CR nor unused storage should appear in the counted output. A direct AH=09h call on line would instead interpret the header as characters and search for a dollar beyond the intended text.

Lecture: 150:00–163:00 (approximate). See sources and corrections.

14 · Application 4: reverse a bounded line using the stack

Last in, first out reverses a sequence naturally. If A, B and C are pushed in that order, the top is C; successive pops return C, B and A. On the 8086 each PUSH/POP here transfers a word.

org 100h
jmp start
prompt db 'Type a line (up to 64 characters): $'
answer db 13,10,'Reversed: $'
line   db 65,0,65 dup(0)
start:
    lea dx, prompt
    mov ah, 09h
    int 21h
    lea dx, line
    mov ah, 0Ah
    int 21h
    xor cx, cx
    mov cl, [line+1]
    mov bx, cx           ; preserve the number of pushed words
    jcxz show_answer
    lea si, line+2
    xor ax, ax
save_char:
    mov al, [si]
    push ax              ; a word per character, not a byte
    inc si
    loop save_char
show_answer:
    lea dx, answer
    mov ah, 09h
    int 21h
    mov cx, bx
    jcxz finish
emit_reverse:
    pop dx
    mov ah, 02h
    int 21h
    loop emit_reverse
finish:
    mov ax, 4C00h
    int 21h
After pushingWords above the original stack topNext popped character
A0041hA
A then B0041h,0042h, with B at the current topB
A then B then C0041h,0042h,0043h, with C at the topC

The program combines the lecture’s stack idea with its buffered-input service. Reading the line first gives a known length, a 64-character bound and DOS editing behavior. The lecture’s streaming AH=01h version demonstrates the same LIFO principle, but a Backspace byte is not automatically an instruction to remove a previously pushed word.

BX records the number of pushed words while the first LOOP consumes CX. Before output, CX is restored from BX. Empty input skips both loops. At the configured maximum, characters occupy 64×2=128 stack bytes, in addition to any service/return frames. Every pushed character is popped before termination.

Lecture: 162:00–178:00 (approximate). See sources and corrections.

15 · Application 5: convert a numeric length into decimal characters

AH=02h outputs a character code, not a numeric quantity. Moving the number 6 into DL does not print '6'; its ASCII code is 36h. Adding 30h works for a single digit 0…9, but a multi-digit value needs a conversion algorithm.

Step for unsigned value 15 decimalQuotientRemainderAction
15 ÷ 1015Push digit 5.
1 ÷ 1001Push digit 1; stop dividing.
Pop in reverse order—1 then 5Add '0' to each and print 31h then 35h.
org 100h
jmp start
prompt db 'Type a line (up to 80 characters): $'
answer db 13,10,'Length: $'
line   db 81,0,81 dup(0)
start:
    lea dx, prompt
    mov ah, 09h
    int 21h
    lea dx, line
    mov ah, 0Ah
    int 21h
    lea dx, answer
    mov ah, 09h
    int 21h
    xor ax, ax
    mov al, [line+1]
    call print_u16
    mov ax, 4C00h
    int 21h

; Input AX=unsigned value. Preserves AX, BX, CX and DX.
print_u16:
    push ax
    push bx
    push cx
    push dx
    xor cx, cx
    mov bx, 10
divide_digits:
    xor dx, dx           ; required before EVERY division
    div bx
    push dx              ; remainder is a digit 0..9
    inc cx
    test ax, ax
    jnz divide_digits
emit_digits:
    pop dx
    add dl, '0'
    mov ah, 02h
    int 21h
    loop emit_digits
    pop dx
    pop cx
    pop bx
    pop ax
    ret

Why DX must be cleared inside the division loop

DIV BX divides the complete DX:AX by BX. After 15÷10, AX=1 and DX=5. Without clearing DX before the next division, the dividend would be 0005:0001h=327681, rather than 1. PUSH DX saves a copy of the remainder; it does not clear DX.

The divide loop executes at least once, so zero produces one digit '0'. Each division pushes one remainder and increments the same digit count; the output loop pops exactly that many words. The helper preserves AX/BX/CX/DX and balances its stack, including its normal near return.

Trace unsigned decimal conversion

Input is decimal, from 0 through 65535. The trace assumes DX=0 before each division, exactly as in print_u16.

15 / 10 → quotient 1, remainder 5; 1 / 10 → quotient 0, remainder 1. Pop 1 then 5 and emit ASCII 31h 35h → 15.

Lecture: 178:00–195:00 (approximate). See sources and corrections.

16 · Test the boundaries, not just the first successful keystroke

Create a separate source file for each complete listing. Use the EXE Hello template for .MODEL/.DATA practice and the COM listings for the five applications. The executable image type, loader assumptions and service environment must agree.

ListingUseful testsExpected result
EXE Hello / COM HelloStart under DOS-compatible execution.Print the greeting with CR/LF and terminate with code 0.
Character echoA, 4 and space as separate runs.The second prompt is followed by the saved byte.
Uppercasea, z, and invalid bytes followed by a valid letter.A/Z; reject out-of-range input before conversion.
Line echoEmpty, ordinary text, embedded dollar, capacity boundary.Emit exactly count bytes.
ReverseEmpty, one character, AB$CD, 64 characters.Empty / same one character / DC$BA / exact reverse; balanced stack.
LengthLengths 0,9,10,15,80. Also test print_u16 separately at 65535.Decimal 0,9,10,15,80 and 65535 without leading zeros.

Localize a failure by checking the interface boundary

  1. Before INT 21h, check AH and all required inputs, especially DS:DX or DL.
  2. After input, inspect AL or the buffer header before calling another service.
  3. For loops, inspect CX in full, the entry condition and the join/exit label.
  4. For stack code, compare SP before and after the whole operation, accounting for active return frames.
  5. For decimal output, inspect AX and DX before every DIV, then the number of pushed digits.

Validation uses assembled 16-bit machine code and a small DOS-service test harness for the five applications and COM Hello. The EXE template’s syntax/layout is checked with the installed emu8086 compiler. The harness models the services relevant to these examples, including an AL-clobbering output call; it is not a full DOS implementation or a test of real keyboard editing, Ctrl-C, redirection or original processor timing.

17 · Worked revision exercises

Predict the bytes, state or output before opening the answer. State the width and the service contract, rather than relying on the visual shape of a mnemonic.

01 · Decode the operation fields

Encode MOV CX,[BX+DI+32DEh] using the register/memory MOV family.

Show worked answer

8B 89 DE 32. Opcode 8Bh has d=1,w=1; ModR/M 89h is 10 001 001; disp16 is DEh then 32h.

02 · Distinguish declaration and constant

How much storage do N EQU 5, X DB 5 and Y DW 5 allocate?

Show worked answer

N allocates no storage merely for the EQU. X allocates one byte, initialized 05h. Y allocates two bytes, 05h then 00h.

03 · Expand nested DUP

Expand DB 4,3,2,2 DUP(1,2 DUP(5),6) and count bytes.

Show worked answer

4,3,2,1,5,5,6,1,5,5,6: eleven bytes. The inner pair of fives is part of each outer repetition.

04 · Index a word matrix

A row-major word matrix has three columns. Give the displacement of row 1,column 2.

Show worked answer

Element index=1×3+2=5. At two bytes per element, the byte displacement is 10 decimal (0Ah).

05 · Find the radix error

Do .STACK 100 and .STACK 100h request the same stack size?

Show worked answer

No. They request 100 decimal and 256 decimal bytes respectively.

06 · Understand ORG

Does ORG 100h execute an instruction that moves IP, or write a 256-byte PSP into the COM file?

Show worked answer

Neither. It sets the assembler’s origin. DOS supplies the PSP and starts execution at the conventional COM entry; the source must still place an instruction at its entry.

07 · Initialize an EXE data segment

Why use MOV AX,@data followed by MOV DS,AX?

Show worked answer

Initial DS refers to the PSP, not necessarily the data group. The data-segment value is established through a general-purpose register because MOV DS,immediate is unavailable.

08 · Avoid fall-through

An if-else assigns CX=1 in the else branch and CX=0 at the then label immediately below it. What is missing?

Show worked answer

A jump from the end of the else path to the common join; otherwise the else result is overwritten by the then assignment.

09 · Handle signed absolute value

What happens when NEG is used on signed word 8000h?

Show worked answer

The stored word remains 8000h and OF=1. It is unsigned magnitude 32768 but cannot represent positive 32768 as a signed 16-bit result.

10 · Respect the DOS register contract

AH=02h is selected. Does a character belong in AL or DL?

Show worked answer

DL. AL is the returned character register for AH=01h; using an input service’s output convention for an output service is a different interface.

11 · Keep a character alive

A character is read into AL, then AH=09h prints a message, then AL is copied into DL. Why can the final character be wrong?

Show worked answer

The string call need not preserve live AL. Save the input in storage or a suitable saved register/stack slot before that call, then restore it for output.

12 · Validate before conversion

Why is subtracting 20h from every input byte not a general uppercase conversion?

Show worked answer

Only ASCII lowercase a…z have the required relationship to A…Z. Digits, controls, extended bytes and other punctuation must be handled separately.

13 · Allocate a line buffer

Reserve a DOS 0Ah buffer for up to 20 user characters.

Show worked answer

Use DB 21,0,21 DUP(?) or separate equivalent declarations: two header bytes plus 21 bytes for text and final CR, 23 bytes total.

14 · Locate the CR

After ABC is returned by function 0Ah, which offsets contain the count, first character and CR?

Show worked answer

Count at +1 is 3; A is at +2; CR is at +5. CR is excluded from the returned count.

15 · Print a literal dollar

Can function 09h print the full input AB$CD after appending another dollar terminator?

Show worked answer

No. It stops at the first dollar, after AB. Output by count with character writes or an appropriate counted-write service.

16 · Budget the reverse stack

How many bytes do 64 pushed character words use, and what if the line is empty?

Show worked answer

128 bytes for characters, plus other active frames. An empty line must skip the push/pop loops so it does not pop unrelated stack data.

17 · Fix repeated division

After 15÷10, AX=1 and DX=5. What is divided if DIV BX runs again with BX=10 and DX unchanged?

Show worked answer

DX:AX is 0005:0001h=327681. Clear DX before dividing the quotient again; pushing the old remainder does not clear it.

18 · Render the zero case

Why should decimal conversion divide zero once rather than skip all work?

Show worked answer

It must emit the character 0. A first division gives quotient 0,remainder 0 and one digit to print; a loop skipped entirely would print nothing.

18 · Knowledge check

Choose one answer for each question. The answer key also works without JavaScript.

1. Which statement allocates one byte?
2. What does DD describe on an 8086?
3. How many user characters fit in a 0Ah input area whose capacity byte is 21?
4. What is DS:DX for AH=09h?
5. Which service takes its output character in DL?
6. Which bytes form a conventional DOS newline?
7. Which operation starts a COM image at its conventional assembled offset?
8. How does a while loop differ from repeat-until?
9. Which branch pair validates an unsigned byte against a…z?
10. Where is the first user character after DOS 0Ah input?
11. What must precede each DIV BX when converting a single unsigned AX by 10?
12. Why push decimal remainders?
Answer key for offline revision and printing

1. B. DB defines a byte; EQU alone allocates no data storage.

2. A. The data size can exceed a native register width without adding new processor registers.

3. C. The capacity includes a final CR, while the returned count excludes it.

4. B. DS supplies the segment and DX supplies the offset.

5. B. Function 02h writes one character; function 01h returns input in AL.

6. C. CR is decimal 13 and LF decimal 10.

7. B. ORG sets the assembly-time address origin.

8. A. A while test may skip the body entirely; repeat-until tests after its body.

9. A. JB/JA express unsigned range comparisons for byte codes.

10. B. The first two bytes are capacity and returned count.

11. C. The dividend is DX:AX; an old remainder must not become its high word.

12. B. Division yields low digits first, and LIFO restores their high-to-low order.

19 · Checklist, sources and corrections

Before runningVerify
Build and loadIs this a COM or MZ EXE, and do its entry point and data-segment setup match?
DataAre element sizes, initial values, string termination and buffer capacity explicit?
Control flowDoes each branch select one result, each loop terminate, and zero count skip unsafe bodies?
CallsAre AH, DS:DX and DL correct for the particular service? Are live values preserved?
StackDo pushes and pops balance, including saved registers, digits and active returns?
RepresentationAre numeric values converted to digit codes, rather than sent as raw control bytes?

Corrections that affect the examples

  • DB/DW/DD are directives but can emit stored bytes. A jump over embedded COM data prevents execution of those bytes as instructions.
  • .STACK with no size and no .STACK directive at all are different cases. A memory model describes organization, not automatic allocation of unlimited storage.
  • DL is an input to DOS character output. An undocumented AL preservation assumption caused the lecture’s first echo failure.
  • Carriage return is 0Dh, linefeed is 0Ah; hexadecimal 10h is not linefeed.
  • A 0Ah input buffer needs a capacity/count header; filling an arbitrary array with dollar does not replace it. Input ends with CR, while 09h output ends with dollar.
  • The reverse program here bounds input and guards the empty case. DOS line editing avoids treating raw Backspace as ordinary pushed text.
  • The decimal routine clears DX on every division and handles zero as one digit. Its digit counter counts every pushed remainder.

Validation scope: browser layout, embedded figures, zoom, quiz, print styles and both tools; assembled 16-bit application code with a focused DOS-service harness; and compilation of the EXE Hello template. A full interactive DOS session, real keyboard editing/redirection and original processor bus/cycle timing were not tested. Later examples announced at the end of the lecture are deferred to the next session.
